modules.title: Python Basics
modules.why:
A language model is just a program that reads text and writes text. Before it can do
anything clever, it has to store text and numbers and show results. That's this module.

modules.title: Control Flow
modules.why:
A language model writes text one character at a time **in a loop**, and training repeats
the same few steps thousands of times. Decisions (`if`) and loops (`for`, `while`) are how
we tell the computer to do that.

modules.title: Data Structures
modules.why:
Inside a language model, text becomes **lists of numbers** (token ids). The vocabulary is
a **dictionary** mapping each character to its id. Counting which character follows which
is literally a dictionary of counts. These containers are the model's raw material.

modules.title: Functions, Files & Text
modules.why:
Functions package steps like `encode(text)` or `train(model)` so we can reuse them.
Language models learn from text files, so we read a real file (some Shakespeare, bundled as
`corpus.txt`) and split it into tokens: words or characters.

modules.title: Classes & Objects
modules.why:
A model is an **object**: it holds data (its parameters, the numbers it learns) and has
abilities (methods like `encode`, `forward` or `generate`). Your autograd engine and every
neural-network layer you build later will be classes.

modules.title: Math for ML (plain Python)
modules.why:
A neural network is mostly **multiplying lists of numbers and adding them up** (dot products
and matrices). A language model outputs **probabilities** for the next character; **softmax**
turns raw scores into probabilities, and the **log** measures how surprised the model was.
That's all the math you need, written as plain Python.

modules.title: Your First Language Model: Bigrams
modules.why:
This **is** a language model. Count which character follows which, turn the counts into
probabilities, sample new text, and measure quality with the loss. Every model up to GPT does
the same three things: **predict next-token probabilities, sample from them, and minimize
the loss**. Only the way the probabilities are computed gets fancier.

modules.title: How Models Learn: Gradients
modules.why:
Counting only works for tiny models. Real language models **learn**: they nudge millions of
numbers (parameters) a little bit at a time in whatever direction lowers the loss. To know that
direction we need **derivatives**, computed automatically by **backpropagation**. Here you build
that engine yourself (a mini version of what PyTorch does), then use it to train neurons.

modules.title: A Neural Language Model
modules.why:
Now we combine everything: a tokenizer, **embeddings** (a learned vector for each character),
an MLP, softmax with cross-entropy loss, and gradient descent with **your** autograd engine.
Instead of looking at one previous character like the bigram model, it looks at several.
This is the architecture of Bengio et al. (2003), the direct ancestor of GPT.

modules.title: Toward Transformers (GPT)
modules.why:
Our MLP sees a fixed window of 3 characters. GPT instead uses **attention**: every position
looks back at *all* previous positions and decides which ones matter. Here you build the core
pieces in pure Python on tiny sizes, so real NumPy/PyTorch transformer code will look familiar.

lessons.title: Your first program: print
lessons.text:
Python runs your code **top to bottom, one line at a time**. `print(...)` shows something on the screen.

- Text (called a **string**) goes inside quotes: `"hello"` or `'hello'`.
- Numbers don't need quotes, and Python does the math first: `print(2 + 3)` shows `5`.
- Give `print` several things separated by commas and it puts spaces between them: `print("total:", 5)` shows `total: 5`.
- `#` starts a **comment**: a note for humans. Python ignores everything after it on that line.

Math symbols: `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide.
lessons.example:
print("Hello, Jacob!")
print(2 + 3)          # Python calculates: 5
print("2 + 3")        # in quotes it's just text: 2 + 3
print("tokens:", 12 * 7)
lessons.task:
Write a program that prints exactly two lines:

1. `Hello, world!`
2. the result of `12 * 7`. Let Python do the math, don't type the answer yourself.
lessons.starter:
# Line 1: print the text Hello, world!

# Line 2: print the result of 12 * 7
lessons.solution:
print("Hello, world!")
print(12 * 7)
lessons.hint: You need two `print(...)` lines. The text needs quotes: `print("Hello, world!")`. The math must **not** be in quotes, or Python will print it as text.
lessons.test:
L = lines()
assert L and L[0] != "", "Nothing was printed. Use print(...) to show output."
assert L[0] == "Hello, world!", f"The first line should be exactly: Hello, world!  (yours: {L[0]})"
assert len(L) >= 2, "I only see one line. Add a second print for 12 * 7."
assert L[1] == "84", f"The second line should be 84 (yours: {L[1]})"
assert "84" not in SRC, "Let Python do the math: write 12 * 7 instead of typing 84."
assert len(L) == 2, "Print exactly two lines."

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.text:
A **variable** is a name that stores a value so you can use it later:

```
x = 5
```

Read `=` as *"gets"*: "x gets 5". It stores a value; it does **not** mean "is equal to".

- Names use lowercase letters, digits and underscores: `vocab_size`, `step2`. No spaces, and they can't start with a digit.
- Use a variable anywhere you'd use its value: `x * 2` is `10`.
- You can update a variable using its old value: `x = x + 1` takes the old `x`, adds 1, and stores the result back.

A language model's settings, like how many different characters it knows (its **vocabulary size**), are stored in variables exactly like this.
lessons.example:
vocab_size = 65        # how many different characters our model knows
context = 8            # how many characters it looks at
total = vocab_size * context
print("total:", total)

vocab_size = vocab_size + 1   # update it
print(vocab_size)             # 66
lessons.task:

2. Create `embedding_dim` that holds `10`.
3. Create `params` equal to `vocab_size` times `embedding_dim`. **Calculate it from the two variables**, don't type the number.
4. Print `params`.
lessons.starter:
vocab_size = 0       # change this
embedding_dim = 0    # change this
# create params here, then print it
lessons.solution:

embedding_dim = 10
params = vocab_size * embedding_dim
print(params)
lessons.hint: `params = vocab_size * embedding_dim`, then `print(params)`.
lessons.test:

assert ns["params"] == 500, "Calculate params from the variables (vocab_size * embedding_dim), don't type 270."

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
lessons.text:
Python has two main kinds of numbers:

- **int**: whole numbers like `7`, `-3`, `1000`
- **float**: numbers with a decimal point like `0.5`, `3.14`, `2.0`

Operators:

- `/` divides and **always gives a float**: `7 / 2` is `3.5`
- `//` divides and rounds down to a whole number: `7 // 2` is `3`
- `%` gives the **remainder**: `7 % 2` is `1`
- `**` is power: `2 ** 3` is `8`

Python follows normal math order (`**` first, then `* / // %`, then `+ -`). Use parentheses to be clear: `(2 + 3) * 4`.

`round(3.14159, 2)` gives `3.14`. `int("42")` turns text into a number, and `float("0.5")` too.

When we train a model we cut text into chunks and batches, which is exactly what `//` and `%` are for.
lessons.task:
We have `total_chars = 1000` characters of text and cut it into chunks of `chunk_size = 64`. Create:

- `full_chunks`: how many **complete** chunks fit (use `//`)
- `leftover`: how many characters are left over (use `%`)
- `average`: `total_chars` divided by `chunk_size` with normal division
- `squared`: `chunk_size` to the power of 2 (use `**`)

Calculate everything from the two variables.
lessons.starter:
total_chars = 1000
chunk_size = 64

full_chunks = 0
leftover = 0
average = 0
squared = 0
lessons.solution:
total_chars = 1000
chunk_size = 64

full_chunks = total_chars // chunk_size
leftover = total_chars % chunk_size
average = total_chars / chunk_size
squared = chunk_size ** 2
lessons.hint: `full_chunks = total_chars // chunk_size`, `leftover = total_chars % chunk_size`, `average = total_chars / chunk_size`, `squared = chunk_size ** 2`.
lessons.test:
assert full_chunks == 15, f"full_chunks should be 15, got {full_chunks!r}"
assert leftover == 40, f"leftover should be 40, got {leftover!r}"
assert approx(average, 15.625), f"average should be 15.625, got {average!r}"
assert squared == 4096, f"squared should be 4096, got {squared!r}"
ns, _ = with_var("total_chars", 200)
assert ns["full_chunks"] == 3 and ns["leftover"] == 8, "Calculate the answers from total_chars and chunk_size, don't type numbers."

lessons.title: Strings: text as a sequence
lessons.text:
A string is a **sequence of characters**. A character-level language model sees text exactly like this: one character after another.

- `len(text)` is the number of characters (spaces count!).
- **Indexing**: `text[0]` is the first character. Counting starts at **0**. `text[-1]` is the last one.
- **Slicing**: `text[2:5]` gives characters at positions 2, 3, 4 (the end is *not* included). `text[:5]` is the first five, `text[5:]` is everything after.
- `+` joins strings, `*` repeats them: `"ab" * 3` is `"ababab"`.
- `text.upper()` / `text.lower()` give an upper/lowercase copy.
- `"cat" in text` is `True` if "cat" appears in the text, otherwise `False`.

`True` and `False` are **booleans**: yes/no values.
lessons.example:
text = "language"
print(len(text))     # 8
print(text[0])       # l
print(text[-1])      # e
print(text[0:4])     # lang
print(text.upper())  # LANGUAGE
print("gua" in text) # True

lessons.title: f-strings and splitting text
lessons.text:
**f-strings** put values inside text. Put `f` before the quote and variables in `{ }`:

```
n = 6
print(f"{n} words")     # 6 words
```

This avoids the classic error `"total: " + 5` (you can't add text and a number). `str(5)` also converts a number into text.

Handy string methods:

- `text.split()` cuts text at spaces and gives a **list** of words: `"a b c".split()` is `['a', 'b', 'c']`
- `"-".join(words)` glues a list of strings together with `-` between them
- `text.replace("a", "b")` replaces every `a` with `b`
- `text.count("the")` counts how many times `"the"` appears
- `text.strip()` removes spaces from both ends

Splitting text into pieces (**tokens**) is the very first step of every language model.
lessons.example:
sentence = "to be or not to be"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)              # ['to', 'be', 'or', 'not', 'to', 'be']
print(len(words))         # 6
print(" | ".join(words))  # to | be | or | not | to | be
print(f"'be' appears {sentence.count('be')} times")

Given `sentence = "the cat sat on the mat"`, create:

- `words`: the list of words (use `.split()`)
- `num_words`: how many words there are
- `joined`: the words joined with `-` between them (`"the-cat-sat-on-the-mat"`)

Then print an f-string so that the output is exactly `6 words` (use `num_words` inside the f-string).

sentence = "the cat sat on the mat"

words = None
num_words = None
joined = None
# print using an f-string
lessons.solution:

lessons.title: Decisions with if / elif / else
lessons.text:
`if` runs a block of code only when a condition is `True`:

```
if score > 90:
    print("great")
elif score > 50:
    print("ok")
else:
    print("keep going")
```

- The line ends with a colon `:`.
- The lines inside are **indented by 4 spaces**. Indentation is how Python knows what's inside the `if`.
- `elif` ("else if") is checked only if the conditions above were False; `else` catches everything left.

Comparisons: `==` equal (two `=`!), `!=` not equal, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.
Combine conditions with `and`, `or`, `not`. `ch in "aeiou"` is True if `ch` is one of those letters.
lessons.task:
Given a single character `ch`, set a variable `kind` to:

- `"vowel"` if `ch` is one of `a e i o u`
- `"space"` if `ch` is a space `" "`
- `"other"` for anything else

Then print `kind`. I'll test your code with several different characters.
lessons.starter:
ch = "e"

# set kind using if / elif / else

print(kind)
lessons.test:
for value, expected in [("e", "vowel"), ("a", "vowel"), ("u", "vowel"), (" ", "space"), ("z", "other"), ("k", "other")]:
    ns, out = with_var("ch", value)
    assert ns.get("kind") == expected, f"For ch = {value!r}, kind should be {expected!r} but got {ns.get('kind')!r}"
    assert expected in lines(out), f"For ch = {value!r} you should print {expected}"

lessons.title: for loops
lessons.text:
A `for` loop repeats a block once **for each item** in a sequence. Looping over a string gives you each character:

```
for ch in "abc":
    print(ch)
```

prints `a`, `b`, `c` on separate lines. The indented block is the **body**; it runs once per item, with `ch` set to the current item.

**The accumulator pattern** is used everywhere: start a variable at 0 *before* the loop, then update it inside:

```
count = 0
for ch in text:
    if ch == "e":
        count = count + 1     # or: count += 1
```

`count += 1` is shorthand for `count = count + 1`.
lessons.task:
Given `text = "attention is all you need"`, use a `for` loop to count:

- `vowels`: how many characters are one of `aeiou`
- `spaces`: how many characters are spaces

Print both numbers.
lessons.starter:
text = "attention is all you need"

vowels = 0
spaces = 0
# loop over the characters of text here

print(vowels, spaces)
lessons.hint: Inside `for ch in text:` add an `if ch in "aeiou":` that does `vowels += 1`, and an `elif ch == " ":` that does `spaces += 1`. Watch the indentation: the `if` is inside the loop (4 spaces), and the `+= 1` is inside the `if` (8 spaces).

lessons.title: range: counting loops
lessons.text:
`range` produces a sequence of numbers to loop over:

- `range(5)` → 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (starts at 0, **stops before** 5)
- `range(1, 6)` → 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
- `range(0, 10, 2)` → 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (the third number is the step)

```
for i in range(3):
    print("step", i)
```

Use it whenever you want to do something a certain number of times, e.g. "train for 100 steps": `for step in range(100):`.

To loop over positions of a string or list: `for i in range(len(text)):` then use `text[i]`.
lessons.task:
Given `n = 10`, use a `for` loop with `range` to compute `total`, the sum of squares:

`1*1 + 2*2 + 3*3 + ... + n*n`

Print `total`. (For n = 10 it's 385.) I'll test other values of `n` too.
lessons.starter:
n = 10

total = 0
# your loop here

print(total)
lessons.solution:
n = 10

total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total += i * i

print(total)
lessons.hint: `range(1, n + 1)` goes from 1 up to and including n. Inside the loop: `total += i * i`.
lessons.test:
assert "range" in SRC, "Use range(...) in a for loop."
assert total == 385, f"For n = 10, total should be 385, got {total!r}"
for n_, exp in [(5, 55), (1, 1), (3, 14)]:
    ns, _ = with_var("n", n_)
    assert ns["total"] == exp, f"For n = {n_}, total should be {exp}, got {ns['total']!r}. Does your range include n itself?"

lessons.title: while loops and break
lessons.text:
A `while` loop repeats **as long as** its condition is True:

```
x = 1
while x < 100:
    x = x * 2
print(x)   # 128
```

The body must eventually make the condition False, or the loop runs forever. (If that happens here, the app stops your program after a few seconds.)

- `break` exits a loop immediately.
- `continue` skips to the next round of the loop.

Training a model often looks like: *keep improving while the loss is still too high*.
lessons.task:
A pretend model starts with `loss = 1.0`. Each training step halves it (`loss = loss * 0.5`).

Use a `while` loop to count in `steps` how many steps it takes until `loss` is **below 0.01**. Print `steps`.
lessons.starter:
loss = 1.0
steps = 0
# your while loop here

print(steps)
lessons.solution:
loss = 1.0
steps = 0
while loss >= 0.01:
    loss = loss * 0.5
    steps += 1

print(steps)
lessons.hint: `while loss >= 0.01:` then, indented, `loss = loss * 0.5` and `steps += 1`.
lessons.test:
assert "while" in SRC, "Use a while loop."
assert steps == 7, f"steps should be 7, got {steps!r}"
assert loss < 0.01, f"After the loop loss should be below 0.01, it is {loss!r}"
ns, _ = with_var("loss", 0.5)
assert ns["steps"] == 6, "Your loop should depend on loss (try starting at 0.5: it should take 6 steps)."

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.text:
A **list** holds many values in order: `nums = [3, 1, 4]`.

- Index and slice just like strings: `nums[0]` is `3`, `nums[-1]` is `4`, `nums[:2]` is `[3, 1]`.
- Lists can be **changed**: `nums[0] = 10`, `nums.append(5)` adds to the end.
- `len(nums)`, `sum(nums)`, `max(nums)`, `min(nums)`, `sorted(nums)` all work.
- `list("abc")` splits a string into characters: `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
- Loop over a list with `for x in nums:`.
- An empty list is `[]`. A common pattern is building a list in a loop with `append`.

A tokenized sentence is just a list: `["h", "e", "l", "l", "o"]` or `[7, 4, 11, 11, 14]`.
lessons.example:
tokens = ["to", "be", "or"]
tokens.append("not")
print(tokens, len(tokens))
print(tokens[1:3])

squares = []
for i in range(5):
    squares.append(i * i)
print(squares, sum(squares))
print(list("hey"))

Starting from `tokens = list("hello")`:

1. Add `"!"` to the end of `tokens` with `append`.
2. `n`: the length of `tokens` (after appending).
3. `first`: the first token.
4. `last_two`: a list of the last two tokens (use a slice).

tokens = list("hello")

# 1. append "!"

n = None
first = None
last_two = None
print(tokens, n, first, last_two)
lessons.solution:

lessons.hint: `tokens.append("!")`, `n = len(tokens)`, `first = tokens[0]`, `last_two = tokens[-2:]`.

assert tokens == ["h", "e", "l", "l", "o", "!"], f"tokens should be ['h','e','l','l','o','!'], got {tokens!r}"
assert n == 6, f"n should be 6, got {n!r}"

assert last_two == ["o", "!"], f"last_two should be ['o', '!'], got {last_two!r}"

assert ns["n"] == 3 and ns["last_two"] == ["b", "!"], "Compute n, first and last_two from tokens."

lessons.title: Dictionaries: counting things
lessons.text:
A **dictionary** maps **keys** to **values**: `ages = {"ann": 31, "bob": 25}`.

- Look up: `ages["ann"]` → `31` (a missing key gives a `KeyError`)
- Add or change: `ages["cy"] = 40`
- Check: `"bob" in ages` → `True`
- Safe lookup with a default: `ages.get("zed", 0)` → `0`
- Loop: `for key, value in ages.items():`

**Counting pattern**, the heart of our first language model:

```
counts = {}
for ch in text:
    counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
```

To find the key with the biggest value: `max(counts, key=counts.get)`.
lessons.task:
Given `text = "banana bread"`:

1. Build a dictionary `counts` mapping each character to how many times it appears (spaces count too).
2. Set `most` to the character with the highest count.
lessons.starter:
text = "banana bread"

counts = {}
# fill counts with a loop

most = None
print(counts, most)
lessons.hint: Inside `for ch in text:` write `counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1`. Then `most = max(counts, key=counts.get)`.
lessons.test:
def ref(t):
    d = {}
    for c in t:
        d[c] = d.get(c, 0) + 1
    return d
assert counts == ref(text), f"counts is not right. Expected {ref(text)!r}, got {counts!r}"
assert most == "a", f"most should be 'a', got {most!r}"
ns, _ = with_var("text", "hello world")
r = ref("hello world")
assert ns["counts"] == r, "counts should be computed from text."
assert ns["most"] == "l", "most should be computed from counts."

lessons.title: Tuples, sets and zip
lessons.text:
**Tuples** are like lists but can't be changed. Written with parentheses: `pair = ("a", "b")`.
You can **unpack** them: `first, second = pair`.

**Sets** hold unique items with no order: `set("hello")` → `{'h', 'e', 'l', 'o'}`. The duplicate `l` is gone.
`sorted(set(text))` gives the **unique characters in order**, which is exactly how we build a vocabulary.

**zip** walks two sequences side by side, giving tuples:

```
list(zip("abc", "bcd"))   # [('a','b'), ('b','c'), ('c','d')]
```

`zip(text, text[1:])` pairs every character with the **next** one. Each pair is a **bigram**, and predicting the second from the first is our first language model.
lessons.example:
text = "hello"
print(set(text))
print(sorted(set(text)))
for a, b in zip(text, text[1:]):
    print(a, "is followed by", b)
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
lessons.task:
Given `text = "hello world"`, create:

- `chars`: a sorted list of the unique characters
- `vocab_size`: how many unique characters there are
- `pairs`: a list of all bigrams, i.e. `(current, next)` tuples, using `zip`
lessons.starter:
text = "hello world"

chars = None
vocab_size = None
pairs = None
print(chars, vocab_size)
print(pairs)
lessons.solution:
text = "hello world"

chars = sorted(set(text))
vocab_size = len(chars)
pairs = list(zip(text, text[1:]))
print(chars, vocab_size)
print(pairs)
lessons.hint: `chars = sorted(set(text))`, `vocab_size = len(chars)`, `pairs = list(zip(text, text[1:]))`.
lessons.test:
for t in ["hello world", "abracadabra"]:
    ns, _ = with_var("text", t)
    assert ns["chars"] == sorted(set(t)), f"For {t!r}, chars should be {sorted(set(t))!r}, got {ns['chars']!r}"

lessons.title: Comprehensions: your first tokenizer
lessons.text:
A **comprehension** builds a list or dictionary in one line:

```
squares = [x * x for x in range(5)]          # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
evens   = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in ["hi", "hello"]}  # {'hi': 2, 'hello': 5}
```

**enumerate** gives positions along with items:

```
for i, ch in enumerate(["a", "b"]):
    print(i, ch)       # 0 a, then 1 b
```

Now the big idea: models only understand **numbers**. A **tokenizer** turns text into numbers and back:

- `stoi` ("string to integer"): `{'a': 0, 'b': 1, ...}`
- `itos` ("integer to string"): `{0: 'a', 1: 'b', ...}`
- **encode**: text → list of ids. **decode**: list of ids → text.
lessons.task:
Given `text = "hello world"` and `chars = sorted(set(text))`, use comprehensions to create:

- `stoi`: dict from each character to its position in `chars`
- `itos`: dict from each position to its character
- `encoded`: the list of ids for every character in `text`
- `decoded`: the text rebuilt from `encoded` (use `"".join(...)` with `itos`)
lessons.starter:
text = "hello world"
chars = sorted(set(text))

stoi = None
itos = None
encoded = None
decoded = None
print(stoi)
print(encoded)
print(decoded)
lessons.solution:
text = "hello world"
chars = sorted(set(text))

stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(chars)}
itos = {i: ch for i, ch in enumerate(chars)}
encoded = [stoi[ch] for ch in text]
decoded = "".join([itos[i] for i in encoded])
print(stoi)
print(encoded)
print(decoded)
lessons.hint: `stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(chars)}`; `itos` is the same with `i: ch`; `encoded = [stoi[ch] for ch in text]`; `decoded = "".join([itos[i] for i in encoded])`.
lessons.test:
for t in ["hello world", "to be or not"]:
    ns, _ = with_var("text", t)
    ch = sorted(set(t))
    st = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(ch)}
    assert ns["stoi"] == st, f"For {t!r}, stoi should be {st}"
    assert ns["itos"] == {i: c for c, i in st.items()}, "itos should map each id back to its character"
    assert ns["encoded"] == [st[c] for c in t], f"encoded should be {[st[c] for c in t]}"
    assert ns["decoded"] == t, "decoded should give back the original text"

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.text:
A **function** is a named, reusable piece of code:

```
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))   # 12
```

- `def` name `(parameters):` then an indented body.
- `return` sends a result back to whoever called the function. **Printing is not returning**: a function without `return` gives back `None`.
- Parameters can have **defaults**: `def greet(name, greeting="Hi"):` lets you call `greet("Jo")`.
- Return several values as a tuple: `return a, b`, and unpack with `x, y = f()`.
- Variables created inside a function only exist inside it.
lessons.task:
Write two functions:

1. `average(nums)`: returns the average (mean) of a list of numbers, i.e. sum divided by count.
2. `split_data(data, frac=0.9)`: splits a list into two parts and returns `(train, val)`. `train` is the first `int(len(data) * frac)` items and `val` is the rest.

We split data like this to test a model on text it **didn't** train on.
lessons.hint: `return sum(nums) / len(nums)`. For split_data: `n = int(len(data) * frac)` then `return data[:n], data[n:]`.
lessons.test:
assert average([1, 2, 3, 4]) == 2.5, f"average([1, 2, 3, 4]) should be 2.5, got {average([1, 2, 3, 4])!r}. Did you return it?"
assert average([10]) == 10
assert approx(average([0.5, 1.5, 4.0]), 2.0)
r = split_data(list(range(10)))
assert r is not None, "split_data returned None. Did you forget return?"
assert list(r[0]) == list(range(9)) and list(r[1]) == [9], f"split_data(list(range(10))) should give ([0..8], [9]), got {r!r}"
tr, va = split_data(list("abcdefghij"), 0.5)
assert list(tr) == list("abcde") and list(va) == list("fghij"), "split_data with frac=0.5 should split in half"

lessons.title: Modules and imports
lessons.text:
Python comes with many **modules** (libraries) you can import:

```
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))     # 4.0
print(math.pi)

import random
random.seed(42)          # make "random" numbers repeatable
print(random.random())   # a float between 0 and 1

from collections import Counter
c = Counter("banana")    # counts everything for you
print(c.most_common(1))  # [('a', 3)]
```

- `import math` then use `math.something`.
- `from module import name` lets you use `name` directly.
- `random.seed(...)` matters in ML: it makes experiments **reproducible**.

Any `.py` file is a module too. Later you'll import `engine.py` and `nn.py` that hold code you wrote.
lessons.example:
import math
from collections import Counter

print(math.sqrt(2), math.exp(1), math.log(math.e))
counts = Counter("mississippi")
print(counts)
print(counts.most_common(2))

2. `distance(x1, y1, x2, y2)`: returns the straight-line distance between two points: the square root of `(x2-x1)**2 + (y2-y1)**2`. Use `math.sqrt`.
lessons.starter:
import math

def most_common_char(text):
    pass


def distance(x1, y1, x2, y2):

print(most_common_char("hello world"))

lessons.title: Reading a text file
lessons.text:
Language models learn from text files. This app bundles some Shakespeare as `corpus.txt`, which you can open by name.

```
with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()
```

- `open(...)` opens the file; `with` makes sure it gets closed afterwards.
- `f.read()` gives the whole file as one string.
- `text.splitlines()` gives a list of lines.
- A newline character is written `"\n"` in Python.

The famous "tiny Shakespeare" dataset Andrej Karpathy used to train small language models is this same kind of text, just bigger.
lessons.example:
with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()

print(len(text), "characters")
print(text[:120])
print(text.splitlines()[:3])
lessons.task:
Read `corpus.txt` into a variable `text`. Then create:

- `num_chars`: number of characters in the text
- `lines_list`: the list of lines (`splitlines`)
- `num_lines`: number of lines
- `first_line`: the first line
lessons.starter:
# read corpus.txt into text

num_chars = None
lines_list = None
num_lines = None
first_line = None
print(num_chars, num_lines, first_line)
lessons.solution:
with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()

num_chars = len(text)
lines_list = text.splitlines()
num_lines = len(lines_list)
first_line = lines_list[0]
print(num_chars, num_lines, first_line)

with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as _f:
    _t = _f.read()

lessons.title: Tokenizing text into words
lessons.text:
**Tokenizing** means splitting text into units the model works with. The simplest choice is words.

Real text is messy: `"Hello, World!"` has capitals and punctuation. A simple word tokenizer:

1. lowercase everything
2. replace every character that isn't a letter with a space (`ch.isalpha()` tells you if `ch` is a letter)
3. `split()` into words

```
"Hello, World!"  ->  "hello  world "  ->  ['hello', 'world']
```

Building a new string character by character: start with `result = ""` and do `result += ch` in a loop, or use `"".join([...])` with a comprehension.

(GPT uses *subword* tokens, chunks between characters and words, but the idea is the same.)
lessons.example:
text = "Speak, speak! You are ALL resolved?"
low = text.lower()
clean = "".join([ch if ch.isalpha() else " " for ch in low])
print(clean)
print(clean.split())
lessons.task:
Write two functions:

1. `tokenize_words(text)`: lowercase the text, replace every non-letter with a space, and return the list of words.
   `tokenize_words("Hello, World! Hello.")` → `['hello', 'world', 'hello']`
2. `word_counts(words)`: given a list of words, return a dictionary mapping each word to how often it appears.
lessons.starter:
def tokenize_words(text):
    pass


def word_counts(words):
    pass


words = tokenize_words("Hello, World! Hello.")
print(words)
print(word_counts(words))
lessons.hint: In tokenize_words: `text = text.lower()`, then build `clean` with `"".join([ch if ch.isalpha() else " " for ch in text])`, then `return clean.split()`. word_counts is the counting pattern from the dictionaries lesson.
lessons.test:
r = tokenize_words("Hello, World! Hello.")
assert r == ["hello", "world", "hello"], f"tokenize_words('Hello, World! Hello.') should be ['hello', 'world', 'hello'], got {r!r}"
r = tokenize_words("We'll  go--NOW")
assert r == ["we", "ll", "go", "now"], f"tokenize_words(\"We'll  go--NOW\") should be ['we', 'll', 'go', 'now'], got {r!r}"
assert tokenize_words("123 !!") == [], "A text with no letters should give []"
c = word_counts(["a", "b", "a"])
assert c == {"a": 2, "b": 1}, f"word_counts(['a','b','a']) should be {{'a': 2, 'b': 1}}, got {c!r}"
assert word_counts([]) == {}

lessons.title: A character tokenizer
lessons.text:
Word tokenizers need huge vocabularies (every word ever!). A **character-level** tokenizer is tiny: the vocabulary is just the set of characters in the text, maybe 60 of them. That's what we'll use for our language models.

Let's package the tokenizer from Module 3 into three reusable functions:

- `build_vocab(text)` → `(stoi, itos)`
- `encode(s, stoi)` → list of ids
- `decode(ids, itos)` → string

A good tokenizer is **lossless**: `decode(encode(s))` gives back exactly `s`.
lessons.example:
with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()
chars = sorted(set(text))
print(len(chars), "unique characters:")
print(repr("".join(chars)))
lessons.task: Write `build_vocab(text)`, `encode(s, stoi)` and `decode(ids, itos)` as described above. The ids should follow the **sorted** order of the unique characters (so in `"hello"`, `e` is 0, `h` is 1, `l` is 2, `o` is 3).
lessons.hint: Reuse your comprehensions: `chars = sorted(set(text))`, `stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(chars)}`, and so on. Don't forget `return stoi, itos`.
lessons.test:
r = build_vocab("hello")
assert r is not None, "build_vocab returned None. Did you forget return stoi, itos?"
s, i = r
assert s == {"e": 0, "h": 1, "l": 2, "o": 3}, f"stoi for 'hello' should be {{'e': 0, 'h': 1, 'l': 2, 'o': 3}}, got {s!r}"
assert i == {0: "e", 1: "h", 2: "l", 3: "o"}, f"itos for 'hello' is wrong: {i!r}"
assert encode("hole", s) == [1, 3, 2, 0], f"encode('hole') should be [1, 3, 2, 0], got {encode('hole', s)!r}"
assert decode([1, 0, 2, 2, 3], i) == "hello", "decode([1, 0, 2, 2, 3]) should be 'hello'"
with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as _f:
    _t = _f.read()
s2, i2 = build_vocab(_t)
assert decode(encode(_t, s2), i2) == _t, "decode(encode(text)) must give back the original corpus"

lessons.title: Classes, objects and __init__
lessons.text:
A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** is a thing built from it.

```
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name        # an attribute
        self.tricks = []

rex = Dog("Rex")      # creates an object, runs __init__
print(rex.name)       # Rex
```

- `__init__` runs automatically when you create an object. It sets up the object's data.
- `self` is the object itself. `self.name = name` stores a value *on the object*.
- Each object has its own attributes: `Dog("Rex")` and `Dog("Fido")` don't share names.

Let's turn our tokenizer into a class that remembers its vocabulary.
lessons.example:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text = text
        self.length = len(text)
        self.unique = len(set(text))

c = Counter("banana")
print(c.text, c.length, c.unique)
lessons.task:
Write a class `Tokenizer`. `Tokenizer(text)` should set these attributes in `__init__`:

- `self.chars`: sorted list of unique characters in `text`
- `self.vocab_size`: how many there are
- `self.stoi`: char → id dictionary
- `self.itos`: id → char dictionary
lessons.hint: Same code as `build_vocab`, but store results on `self`: `self.chars = sorted(set(text))`, `self.vocab_size = len(self.chars)`, and so on.
lessons.test:
t = Tokenizer("hello")
assert getattr(t, "chars", None) == ["e", "h", "l", "o"], f"Tokenizer('hello').chars should be ['e','h','l','o'], got {getattr(t, 'chars', None)!r}"
assert getattr(t, "vocab_size", None) == 4, "vocab_size should be 4 for 'hello'"
assert getattr(t, "stoi", None) == {"e": 0, "h": 1, "l": 2, "o": 3}, "stoi is wrong"
assert getattr(t, "itos", None) == {0: "e", 1: "h", 2: "l", 3: "o"}, "itos is wrong"
t2 = Tokenizer("ab")
assert t2.vocab_size == 2 and t.vocab_size == 4, "Each Tokenizer should have its own attributes"

lessons.title: Methods
lessons.text:
A **method** is a function that belongs to a class. Its first parameter is always `self`, so it can use the object's attributes:

```
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def speak(self, times=1):
        return (self.name + " says woof! ") * times

rex = Dog("Rex")
print(rex.speak(2))     # Python passes rex as self automatically
```

Methods can call other methods with `self.other_method(...)`.
lessons.task:
Add two methods to `Tokenizer`:

- `encode(self, s)`: returns the list of ids for string `s`
- `decode(self, ids)`: returns the string for a list of ids
lessons.hint:
```
    def encode(self, s):
        return [self.stoi[ch] for ch in s]
```
Indent `def` by 4 spaces so it's inside the class. decode is similar, using `"".join(...)` and `self.itos`.
lessons.test:
t = Tokenizer("hello")
assert hasattr(t, "encode"), "Tokenizer needs an encode method (indented inside the class)"
assert hasattr(t, "decode"), "Tokenizer needs a decode method (indented inside the class)"
assert t.encode("hole") == [1, 3, 2, 0], f"encode('hole') should be [1, 3, 2, 0], got {t.encode('hole')!r}"
assert t.decode([1, 0, 2, 2, 3]) == "hello", f"decode([1, 0, 2, 2, 3]) should be 'hello', got {t.decode([1, 0, 2, 2, 3])!r}"
with open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8") as _f:
    _t = _f.read()
tc = Tokenizer(_t)
assert tc.decode(tc.encode(_t)) == _t, "decode(encode(corpus)) should give back the corpus"

lessons.title: Special methods: making + work
lessons.text:
Python lets your objects work with operators by defining **special methods** (also called "dunder" methods, for the double underscores):

- `__add__(self, other)` runs for `a + b`
- `__mul__(self, other)` runs for `a * b`
- `__len__(self)` runs for `len(a)`
- `__repr__(self)` decides how the object looks when printed

```
class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents
    def __add__(self, other):
        return Money(self.cents + other.cents)   # a NEW object
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Money({self.cents})"

print(Money(5) + Money(10))    # Money(15)
```

This trick is the key to Module 8: we'll make a `Value` class where `a * b + c` secretly records the calculation so it can compute derivatives.
lessons.task:
Write a class `Vector` holding a list of numbers in `self.values`:

- `Vector([1, 2]) + Vector([3, 4])` → `Vector([4, 6])` (add element by element)
- `Vector([1, 2]) * 3` → `Vector([3, 6])` (multiply each element by a number)
- `len(Vector([1, 2, 3]))` → `3`
- `repr(Vector([1, 2]))` → the text `Vector([1, 2])`

`+` and `*` must return **new** `Vector` objects.
lessons.starter:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, values):
        self.values = list(values)

    # add __add__, __mul__, __len__, __repr__


print(Vector([1, 2]) + Vector([3, 4]))
print(Vector([1, 2]) * 3)
print(len(Vector([1, 2, 3])))
lessons.hint: `__add__` can use `zip`: `Vector([a + b for a, b in zip(self.values, other.values)])`. `__repr__` should `return f"Vector({self.values})"`.
lessons.test:
a, b = Vector([1, 2]), Vector([3, 4])
c = a + b
assert isinstance(c, Vector), "a + b should return a new Vector"
assert c.values == [4, 6], f"Vector([1, 2]) + Vector([3, 4]) should have values [4, 6], got {c.values!r}"
assert a.values == [1, 2], "+ must not change the original vectors"
d = a * 3
assert isinstance(d, Vector) and d.values == [3, 6], "Vector([1, 2]) * 3 should be Vector([3, 6])"
assert len(Vector([1, 2, 3])) == 3, "len(Vector([1, 2, 3])) should be 3"
assert repr(Vector([1, 2])) == "Vector([1, 2])", f"repr should be 'Vector([1, 2])', got {repr(Vector([1, 2]))!r}"

lessons.title: Vectors and the dot product
lessons.text:
In ML a **vector** is just a list of numbers, like `[0.2, -1.0, 0.5]`. Each character in a model gets its own vector.

- **Adding** vectors: add matching elements. `[1, 2] + [3, 4]` → `[4, 6]`
- **Scaling**: multiply every element. `[1, 2] * 3` → `[3, 6]`
- **Dot product**: multiply matching elements and **add them all up**:

```
dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]) = 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32
```

The dot product measures how much two vectors "agree". It's the single most important operation in deep learning: every neuron computes a dot product, and attention in GPT is built from dot products.

`zip(a, b)` pairs up matching elements, perfect for this.
lessons.example:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [4, 5, 6]
pairs = list(zip(a, b))
print(pairs)
print(sum([x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)]))   # 32
lessons.task:
Write three functions working on lists of numbers:

- `dot(a, b)`: the dot product (a single number)
- `add(a, b)`: element-wise sum (a new list)
- `scale(v, k)`: every element of `v` times the number `k` (a new list)
lessons.hint: `return sum([x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)])`. add is the same comprehension without `sum` and with `+`.
lessons.test:
assert dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]) == 32, f"dot([1,2,3],[4,5,6]) should be 32, got {dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])!r}"
assert dot([1, 0], [0, 1]) == 0
assert approx(dot([0.5, -1.0], [2.0, 3.0]), -2.0)
assert add([1, 2], [3, 4]) == [4, 6], f"add([1,2],[3,4]) should be [4, 6], got {add([1, 2], [3, 4])!r}"
assert scale([1, 2], 3) == [3, 6], f"scale([1,2],3) should be [3, 6], got {scale([1, 2], 3)!r}"
v = [1, 2]
scale(v, 5)
assert v == [1, 2], "scale should return a new list, not change the original"

lessons.title: Matrices as lists of lists
lessons.text:
A **matrix** is a grid of numbers: a list of rows, where each row is a list.

```
M = [[1, 2, 3],
     [4, 5, 6]]      # 2 rows, 3 columns
M[1][2]              # row 1, column 2 → 6
```

**Creating a zero matrix**: use a comprehension, `[[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]`.
⚠️ Don't write `[[0] * cols] * rows`: that makes every row the *same* list, so changing one row changes all of them!

**Matrix × vector**: the dot product of each row with the vector:

```
matvec([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [1, 1]) = [1+2, 3+4] = [3, 7]
```

A neural network layer is exactly this: a matrix of weights times an input vector.

**Transpose** flips rows and columns: row `i`, column `j` becomes row `j`, column `i`.
lessons.example:
M = [[1, 2, 3],
     [4, 5, 6]]
print(len(M), "rows,", len(M[0]), "columns")
print(M[1][2])

bad = [[0] * 2] * 2
bad[0][0] = 9
print("the trap:", bad)       # both rows changed!
good = [[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)]
good[0][0] = 9
print("correct: ", good)
lessons.task:
Write:

- `zeros(rows, cols)`: a matrix of zeros with independent rows
- `matvec(M, v)`: matrix times vector (a list with one dot product per row)
- `transpose(M)`: the transposed matrix

A `dot(a, b)` function is provided for you.
lessons.hint: `matvec`: `[dot(row, v) for row in M]`. `transpose`: a nested comprehension, `[[M[r][c] for r in range(len(M))] for c in range(len(M[0]))]` (or the shortcut `[list(col) for col in zip(*M)]`).
lessons.test:
z = zeros(2, 3)
assert z == [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], f"zeros(2, 3) should be [[0,0,0],[0,0,0]], got {z!r}"
z[0][0] = 1
assert z[1][0] == 0, "The rows of zeros() must be independent lists (see the trap in the lesson)"

assert matvec([[1, 0, 2]], [3, 4, 5]) == [13]

lessons.title: Probability and sampling
lessons.text:
A language model outputs a **probability distribution**: one number per possible next character, each between 0 and 1, all adding up to 1.

**Normalizing** turns counts into probabilities: divide each count by the total.
`[2, 6, 2]` → `[0.2, 0.6, 0.2]`

**Sampling** means picking an index at random *according to* those probabilities. Index 1 above should be picked 60% of the time. How? Take a random number `r` between 0 and 1 and walk through the probabilities, adding them up:

```
probs = [0.2, 0.6, 0.2]   running total: 0.2, 0.8, 1.0
r = 0.5  →  0.5 < 0.2? no.  0.5 < 0.8? yes → pick index 1
```

Python's `random` module does this for you with `random.choices(range(3), weights=probs)[0]`, but now you know what it does inside.
lessons.example:
import random
random.seed(0)
probs = [0.2, 0.6, 0.2]
picks = [random.choices(range(3), weights=probs)[0] for _ in range(1000)]
for i in range(3):
    print(i, picks.count(i) / 1000)   # close to 0.2, 0.6, 0.2

- `sample_index(probs, r)`: given probabilities and a number `r` (0 ≤ r < 1), walk through the running total and return the first index `i` where `r < running_total`. If rounding means you never hit it, return the last index.

lessons.title: exp and softmax
lessons.text:
A neural network outputs raw scores called **logits**, any numbers like `[2.0, 1.0, -1.0]`. We need probabilities. **Softmax** converts them:

1. take `math.exp(x)` of each score (e ≈ 2.718 to the power x). This makes everything positive, and bigger scores become *much* bigger.
2. divide each by the total so they add up to 1.

```
logits  [2.0, 1.0, -1.0]
exp     [7.39, 2.72, 0.37]   total 10.48
softmax [0.705, 0.259, 0.035]
```

**Stability trick**: `math.exp(1000)` overflows. Subtracting the largest logit from every logit first doesn't change the answer (the factor cancels out) but keeps the numbers small. Every real implementation does this.

logits = [2.0, 1.0, -1.0]

total = sum(exps)
print([round(e / total, 3) for e in exps])
lessons.task: Write `softmax(logits)` that returns the list of probabilities. Subtract `max(logits)` from every logit before calling `math.exp`, so that `softmax([1000, 1000])` works and gives `[0.5, 0.5]`.

    pass

print(softmax([1000, 1000]))

def softmax(logits):
    m = max(logits)
    exps = [math.exp(x - m) for x in logits]
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]


print(softmax([2.0, 1.0, -1.0]))
print(softmax([1000, 1000]))

lessons.title: log and cross-entropy loss
lessons.text:
How do we score a prediction? Say the model gave the *correct* next character probability `p`.

- `p = 1.0` → perfect. `p = 0.01` → terrible.

The **negative log likelihood** is `-math.log(p)`:

| p | -log(p) |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | 0.0 |
| 0.5 | 0.69 |
| 0.1 | 2.30 |
| 0.01 | 4.61 |

It's 0 when the model is certain and right, and grows as the model gets more surprised. Applying it to softmax(logits) is called **cross-entropy loss**. Training any language model, including GPT, means **making this number small**, averaged over lots of examples.

A useful reference point: guessing uniformly among `V` characters gives a loss of `log(V)`.

    print(p, round(-math.log(p), 3))
print("uniform guess over 27 chars:", math.log(27))

lessons.title: Counting bigrams
lessons.text:
Our first model's rule: **predict the next character using only the current character.**

To learn it, count every bigram (pair of neighbours) in the text. We store the counts in a `V × V` matrix `N` (`V` = vocabulary size):

`N[i][j]` = how many times character `itos[i]` was followed by character `itos[j]`.

```
text "abab":  pairs (a,b) (b,a) (a,b)
           next: a  b
      a  [ [0, 2],
      b    [1, 0] ]
```

Row `i` is everything we know about what follows character `i`. That row **is** the model's knowledge.

V = len(chars)

lessons.title: From counts to probabilities
lessons.text:
Turn each row of counts into probabilities by dividing by the row's total. Now `P[i][j]` = probability that `itos[j]` comes next after `itos[i]`.

**Smoothing problem**: if a pair never appeared, its probability is 0, and `-log(0)` is infinity, so one unseen pair would make the loss infinite. The fix: pretend we saw every pair `smoothing` extra times (usually 1) before dividing:

```
P[i][j] = (N[i][j] + smoothing) / (sum(N[i]) + smoothing * V)
```

This is called *add-one* (Laplace) smoothing. Neural networks get this kind of thing for free because softmax never outputs exactly 0.
lessons.example:

total = sum(row)
print([c / total for c in row])                 # unsmoothed: has a 0
print([(c + 1) / (total + 3) for c in row])     # smoothed: no zeros

def counts_to_probs(N, smoothing=1):

lessons.title: Sampling new text
lessons.text:
Now the fun part: **generate text**. Start from a character and repeat:

1. look up the probability row for the current character
2. sample the next character from it
3. that character becomes the current one

```
current = start
repeat:
    row = P[stoi[current]]
    idx = rng.choices(range(len(row)), weights=row)[0]
    current = itos[idx]
```

`rng = random.Random(seed)` is a private random generator: the same seed always gives the same text, which makes results reproducible.

The output will look like gibberish with Shakespeare-ish spacing and capitals. That's what a model that only remembers *one* character can do. Making it remember more is the story of the rest of this course.
lessons.example:

print([rng.choices(["a", "b", "c"], weights=[0.7, 0.2, 0.1])[0] for _ in range(10)])

    for a, b in zip(text, text[1:]):
        N[stoi[a]][stoi[b]] += 1
    return N

    for row in N:

lessons.title: Measuring the model: loss
lessons.text:
Is our model any good? Use the **average negative log likelihood** from Module 6: for every bigram `(a, b)` in some text, see what probability the model gave `b` after `a`, and average `-log` of it:

```
loss = average of  -log(P[stoi[a]][stoi[b]])  over all pairs
```

Lower is better. Reference points for this corpus:

- uniform random guessing: `log(V)` ≈ 4.03 (V = 56 characters)
- our bigram model: somewhere around 2.4 to 2.5
- a big transformer on lots of Shakespeare: ≈ 1.0 to 1.5

When you hear "the loss went down" in ML news, this is the number they mean.

1. Split the text: first 90% for **training**, last 10% for **validation**.

    P = []
    for row in N:
        total = sum(row) + smoothing * len(row)
        P.append([(c + smoothing) / total for c in row])
    return P

        current = itos[idx]
        out.append(current)
    return "".join(out)

    n = 0
    for a, b in zip(text, text[1:]):

        n += 1
    return total / n

lessons.title: Derivatives: which way is downhill?
lessons.text:
The **derivative** of a function at a point tells you: *if I nudge the input up a tiny bit, how much does the output change, and in which direction?*

For `f(x) = x**2` at `x = 3`: nudge x to 3.001 and f goes from 9 to 9.006001. The output changed about **6 times** as much as the input, so the derivative (slope) is 6.

We can estimate it with a tiny step `h`:

```
derivative ≈ (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h)
```

Why we care: if the derivative of the **loss** with respect to some parameter is positive, increasing that parameter increases the loss, so we should **decrease** it. Derivatives tell every parameter which way to move. That's all of deep learning.

Functions can be passed around like values: `numerical_derivative(f, 3.0)` hands the function `f` itself to another function.

3. Set `slope_g` to the numerical derivative of `g` at `x = 2.0` (it should be close to 8).

lessons.title: The Value class: remembering the math
lessons.text:
Numerical derivatives are slow (two function calls per parameter) and imprecise. Instead, we'll make numbers that **remember how they were made**, so the derivatives can be worked out exactly.

A `Value` wraps a number:

- `data`: the number itself
- `grad`: its derivative (filled in later, starts at 0)
- `_prev`: the Values it was made from (its "children")
- `_op`: the operation that made it (`"+"` or `"*"`)

Using `__add__` and `__mul__` (Module 5), `a * b + c` creates a whole **graph** of Values linking the result back to `a`, `b` and `c`.

To allow `Value(2) + 1`, convert plain numbers first:
`other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)`.

lessons.title: Backpropagation
lessons.text:
Now fill in the gradients. We want `x.grad` = *how much the final output changes if `x` is nudged*. Two local rules, combined by the **chain rule**:

- `out = a + b`: nudging `a` nudges `out` by the same amount, so `a.grad += out.grad` and `b.grad += out.grad`
- `out = a * b`: nudging `a` changes `out` by `b` times as much, so `a.grad += b.data * out.grad` and `b.grad += a.data * out.grad`

Each new Value gets a small `_backward` function that applies its rule. Note it's `+=`, not `=`: a Value used twice collects gradient from both uses.

`backward()` on the final result:

1. sets its own `grad` to 1 (the output changes 1:1 with itself)
2. puts all Values in **topological order** (each Value after the ones it was made from)
3. calls `_backward()` on each, **from the output back to the inputs**

That's backpropagation, exactly what `loss.backward()` does in PyTorch.

lessons.title: More operations: pow and tanh
lessons.text:
Neural networks need a few more operations, each with its own local derivative rule:

- `out = x ** k` (k a plain number): derivative `k * x**(k-1)`, so `self.grad += k * self.data ** (k - 1) * out.grad`
- `out = tanh(x)`: squashes any number into (-1, 1). Its derivative is `1 - tanh(x)**2`, so `self.grad += (1 - t * t) * out.grad` where `t` is the output

Others come for free by combining existing ones: `-x` is `x * -1`, `a - b` is `a + (-b)`, `a / b` is `a * b**-1`. We also add `__radd__`/`__rmul__` so `1 + x` and `sum([...])` work.

The finished engine (with `exp` and `log` too) is saved as **engine.py**, so later lessons can just write `from engine import Value`.

lessons.title: Gradient descent
lessons.text:
Now we can **learn**. The recipe, repeated many times:

1. **Forward**: compute the loss from the current parameters.
2. **Zero the grads**: set every parameter's `grad` to 0 (they accumulate with `+=`!).
3. **Backward**: `loss.backward()` fills in each parameter's gradient.
4. **Update**: move each parameter a small step *against* its gradient: `p.data -= learning_rate * p.grad`

Let's fit a line. The data was made with `y = 2x + 1`; the model `w * x + b` starts with `w = 0, b = 0` and must discover 2 and 1. The loss is the **mean squared error**: the average of `(prediction - target)**2`.

From now on we import the finished engine: `from engine import Value`.

lessons.title: A neuron
lessons.text:
A **neuron** is the building block of neural networks:

1. take inputs `x1, x2, ...`
2. multiply each by a **weight** `w1, w2, ...` and add a **bias** `b`, i.e. a dot product plus b
3. pass the result through a **nonlinearity**, here `tanh`

```
out = tanh(w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + b)
```

The weights and bias are the **parameters**: the numbers learning will adjust. Start the weights at small random values (`random.uniform(-1, 1)`) so different neurons learn different things.

`sum(list_of_values, start)` adds everything to `start`. With Values, `sum((wi * xi for ...), self.b)` builds the whole dot product plus bias.

lessons.title: A neural network (MLP) that learns
lessons.text:
Stack neurons into **layers**, and layers into a **multi-layer perceptron (MLP)**:

- a **Layer** is a list of neurons that all see the same inputs
- an **MLP** feeds each layer's outputs into the next layer

`nn.py` contains `Neuron`, `Layer` and `MLP` built just like yours. `MLP(3, [4, 4, 1])` means 3 inputs → 4 neurons → 4 neurons → 1 output (the last layer has no tanh, so it can output any number). It has 41 parameters.

Training is the same recipe as gradient descent, just with more parameters:

```
loss = ...                     # forward
model.zero_grad()              # sets every p.grad = 0
loss.backward()
for p in model.parameters():
    p.data -= lr * p.grad
```

This tiny network learns to output the right target for 4 examples. A language model is the same thing with far more parameters, inputs and examples.

print(len(model.parameters()), "parameters")

4. append `loss.data` to `losses`

lessons.title: Building a training dataset
lessons.text:
The bigram model only saw **one** previous character. Our neural model will see `block_size` previous characters (say 3) and predict the next one.

So we turn the text into training examples: each **context** of 3 ids, and the **target** id that follows.

```
text:  "the cat"        block_size = 3
"the" -> " "
"he " -> "c"
"e c" -> "a"
" ca" -> "t"
```

`X` is the list of contexts and `Y` the list of targets. A sliding window over the text: for each start position `i`, the context is `ids[i : i + block_size]` and the target is `ids[i + block_size]`.

To keep things small and fast, `lmdata.load_text()` lowercases the corpus and keeps only letters and spaces, a vocabulary of 27 characters.

lessons.title: Embeddings
lessons.text:
A neural network needs numbers, but a character id like `7` isn't meaningful as a quantity (`h` isn't "more" than `g`). So each character gets its own **embedding**: a small vector of numbers that the model **learns**.

All embeddings live in a table `C` with one row per character (`V` rows × `emb_dim` columns). Looking up character `i` is just `C[i]`.

For a context of 3 characters, we look up all 3 embeddings and join them into one list of `3 × emb_dim` numbers. That's the MLP's input.

During training, characters that behave similarly (like vowels) tend to end up with similar embedding vectors. GPT works the same way: its first layer is an embedding table, just much bigger (50,000 tokens × 768+ numbers).

lessons.title: Softmax + cross-entropy with Values
lessons.text:
The MLP outputs `V` logits (Values). To train, we need the cross-entropy loss **as a Value**, so `loss.backward()` can send gradients all the way back into the MLP and the embeddings.

Same math as Module 6, using Value operations:

1. `m = max(l.data for l in logits)` (a plain number, for stability)
2. `exps = [(l - m).exp() for l in logits]`
3. `total = sum(exps)`
4. `prob = exps[target] / total`
5. `loss = -prob.log()`

This creates lots of tiny nodes, which is slow in pure Python. So `engine.py` also has `cross_entropy(logits, target)`, a **fused** version that gives the same number and the same gradients in one node, with the derivative worked out on paper: `grad of logit i = prob_i - (1 if i is the target else 0)`. PyTorch's `F.cross_entropy` does exactly this. We'll use the fused one for training.
lessons.example:

logits = [Value(2.0), Value(1.0), Value(-1.0)]
loss = cross_entropy(logits, 0)
loss.backward()
print(loss)
print([round(l.grad, 4) for l in logits])   # prob_i - 1 for the target

from engine import Value, cross_entropy


def loss_fn(logits, target):
    m = max(l.data for l in logits)
    exps = [(l - m).exp() for l in logits]
    total = sum(exps)
    prob = exps[target] / total
    return -prob.log()


logits = [Value(2.0), Value(1.0), Value(-1.0)]
loss = loss_fn(logits, 0)
print(loss)

lessons.title: Training the neural language model
lessons.text:
Everything is set up for you: the dataset `X, Y`, the embedding table `C`, the `model`, a `forward(context)` function that returns logits, the list of all `params`, and `evaluate(indices)` for measuring loss.

Training uses **mini-batches**: each step looks at a random handful of examples (here 16) rather than all 6,000+. It's much faster and works nearly as well. Every step:

1. pick a random batch of example indices from the training part (`rng.sample(range(n_train), batch_size)`)
2. loss = average `cross_entropy(forward(X[i]), Y[i])` over the batch
3. zero all grads, `loss.backward()`
4. update all params: `p.data -= lr * p.grad`

The bigram model scored about **2.30** validation loss on this lowercase text, and random guessing scores log(27) ≈ 3.30. With these quick settings (300 steps, a few seconds) the network gets to about the bigram's level. Raise `steps` to 1500 and `hidden` to 48 and click **Run** (it takes a minute or so) and it beats the bigram, reaching about 2.1, because it sees 3 characters instead of 1.

lessons.title: Generating text with the neural model
lessons.text:
Sampling works like the bigram model, except the context is the last `block_size` characters and the probabilities come from the network:

```
context = [stoi[" "]] * block_size      # start with spaces
repeat:
    logits = forward(context)
    probs  = softmax of the logits' .data values
    idx    = rng.choices(range(V), weights=probs)[0]
    output the character itos[idx]
    context = context[1:] + [idx]       # slide the window
```

`context[1:] + [idx]` drops the oldest character and adds the new one.

**Temperature** is a common knob: divide the logits by `temperature` before softmax. Below 1 the text gets more predictable, above 1 more random. ChatGPT has the same setting.

The training loop from the last lesson is included (it takes a few seconds before your function runs).

lessons.title: Embeddings, similarity and positions
lessons.text:
Two more embedding ideas that transformers rely on:

**1. Similarity.** Since every token is a vector, we can measure how alike two tokens are. **Cosine similarity** is the dot product divided by both lengths:

```
cosine(a, b) = dot(a, b) / (length(a) * length(b))     length(v) = sqrt(dot(v, v))
```

It's 1 for vectors pointing the same way, 0 for unrelated (perpendicular) ones, and -1 for opposites. Trained embeddings put similar words close together: "king" near "queen".

**2. Positions.** Attention (next lesson) treats its inputs as an unordered set, so on its own it can't tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog". GPT fixes this with a second table of **position embeddings**, one vector per position (0, 1, 2, ...), and simply **adds** it to each token's embedding:

```
x[t] = token_emb[ids[t]] + pos_emb[t]      (element by element)
```

- `embed_sequence(ids, token_emb, pos_emb)`: a list with one vector per position `t`: `token_emb[ids[t]]` plus `pos_emb[t]`, element by element

import math


def cosine(a, b):
    d = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    la = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    lb = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in b))
    return d / (la * lb)


def embed_sequence(ids, token_emb, pos_emb):
    return [[t + p for t, p in zip(token_emb[i], pos_emb[pos])] for pos, i in enumerate(ids)]

lessons.title: Attention
lessons.text:
**Attention** lets one position gather information from others, weighting each by relevance. Each position has three vectors:

- a **query** `q`: what am I looking for?
- a **key** `k`: what do I contain?
- a **value** `v`: what will I hand over if chosen?

For one query and a list of keys and values:

1. **scores**: `dot(q, k) / sqrt(d)` for every key (`d` = vector length; dividing keeps the numbers from getting too big)
2. **weights** = `softmax(scores)`: they add up to 1
3. **output** = weighted sum of the values: `sum(weights[s] * values[s])`, element by element

If a key matches the query well, its value dominates the output. That's the whole trick, and the "Attention" in the paper title *Attention Is All You Need*.

    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]


def matvec(M, v):
    return [dot(row, v) for row in M]

keys = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]

lessons.title: Causal self-attention
lessons.text:
In **self-attention**, a sequence attends to itself. Every position `t` makes its own query, key and value by multiplying its vector `x[t]` by three **learned** weight matrices:

```
q[t] = matvec(Wq, x[t])     k[t] = matvec(Wk, x[t])     v[t] = matvec(Wv, x[t])
```

For a language model there's one rule: **no peeking at the future**. Position `t` may only attend to positions `0..t`, because when generating, later characters don't exist yet. This is called **causal** (or masked) attention.

So the output at position `t` is `attention(q[t], k[0..t], v[0..t])`.

A real GPT runs several of these in parallel (**multi-head** attention), each with its own matrices, and joins the results.

lessons.title: Capstone: a tiny GPT, and where to go next
lessons.text:
You now know every ingredient of GPT. Here's the whole architecture:

1. **Token + position embeddings** → one vector `x[t]` per position
2. **Transformer blocks**, repeated N times (GPT-2 small: 12). Each block:
   - `x = x + self_attention(layer_norm(x))` (tokens share information)
   - `x = x + mlp(layer_norm(x))` (each position "thinks" on its own)
   - The `x + ...` is a **residual connection**: each block adds a small update instead of replacing `x`, which makes deep networks trainable. **Layer norm** rescales each vector to a stable size.
3. **Output layer**: `logits[t] = matvec(W_out, x[t])`, scores for the next token at every position
4. **Loss**: cross-entropy against the actual next tokens, trained with gradient descent and backprop. You built every piece!

**Next steps** (when you have internet):

- NumPy, for fast math on whole matrices at once: [NumPy quickstart](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/quickstart.html)
- PyTorch, the same `Value`/`backward()` idea on big tensors and GPUs: [Learn the Basics](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/intro.html)
- Andrej Karpathy's [Neural Networks: Zero to Hero](https://karpathy.ai/zero-to-hero.html) video course rebuilds micrograd, makemore and GPT, the exact path this app followed
- [micrograd](https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd) and [nanoGPT](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT), small and readable reference code
- [The Illustrated Transformer](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/) explains attention with pictures
- The original paper: [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

Suggested project: port Module 9 to PyTorch, then swap the MLP for transformer blocks. That's nanoGPT.
